claims.text: Progressive creep deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is primarily governed by interface-mediated dislocation processes.
Interface chemistry modulates local lattice distortion and short-range order.
Nanoscale interface thickness modulates local lattice distortion and short-range order.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order control dislocation nucleation, glide, and climb.
The interplay of intralayer dislocation slip and interface-enhanced diffusion and climb explains progressive deformation under sustained loading.
The starting coatings possess a well-defined FCC/BCC nanoscale layered microstructure.
Systematic variation of interlayer thickness and interface chemistry can deliberately alter lattice misfit and local short-range order.
Elevated-temperature creep conditions promote atomic diffusion and dislocation activity.
Interface composition and spacing mediate dislocation nucleation and climb through their effects on lattice distortion and short-range order.
Under sustained high-temperature loading, dislocations nucleate within the individual FCC and BCC layers.
Interfaces with tuned chemistry, lower lattice misfit, and enhanced short-range order pin dislocations.
Those same modified interfaces facilitate diffusion-assisted dislocation climb.
Interface-mediated pinning and climb balance strengthening with deformation tolerance by enabling controlled migration and recovery.
Reduced interface misfit is expected to lower the creep rate relative to the baseline multilayer.
Enhanced local ordering is expected to lower the creep rate relative to the baseline multilayer.
Increased interlayer thickness is expected to lower the creep rate relative to the baseline multilayer.
Optimized interfaces are expected to produce more stable dislocation configurations and a lower density of rapidly propagating dislocations.
Interfaces with higher misfit and less local order are expected to deform more rapidly under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer structure remains intact and the loading remains within the high-temperature creep regime.
A lack of systematic changes in creep rate and interface-mediated dislocation activity after changing thickness and chemistry would falsify interface-mediated dominance.
